newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-Newcrest clears decks, sees bankers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Newcrest clears decks, sees bankers.

text.p: Australian gold miner Newcrest Mining Ltd on Wednesday trimmed its biggest asset down to size, wiping A$100 million off the value of its troubled Telfer mine to help convince bankers to invest in the company's future.
Newcrest chief executive Ian Johnson, just six weeks into the job, also announced the company had almost halved the mine's production outlook and revised expansion plans at the site.
"We could not have serious dialogue on funding with the banks unless we had Telfer right, because it would have been a pointless exercise," Johnson told reporters.

Newcrest is looking to spend about A$550 million over the next 18 months to develop the Cadia project in Australia's New South Wales state and the smaller Gosowong project in Indonesia, as well as to assess the feasibility of a third project.
The third project, at Ridgeway near the Cadia project, would require Newcrest in about two years to spend in the order of A$150 million to A$200 million, Johnson said.

Newcrest is looking at all its funding options, including the possible sale of its interest in two small Australian gold mines, a 22.22 percent share of production in the Boddington mine and an 80 percent share of the New Celebration mine.
"We have not ruled out any of these options," he said.
Getting the Telfer mine into shape is critical if Newcrest is to convince its bankers to stump up the development funds and fuel the company's future growth, Johnson said.
After the write-down, Telfer will have a book value of A$191 million. Its production forecast of 600,000 ounces by 1998 has been slashed to 300,000 ounces in the year ending June 30, 1998.
Newcrest predicts the unprofitable mine will start making a return in 1997/98. Production will then average about 350,000 ounces for the three years from 1998/99, it said.
Capital expenditure budgeted for the open-pit mine has also been slashed to around just A$30 million to A$40 million over the next five years, as Newcrest shelves underground expansion.
"Underground mining is not capable of sustaining significantly more than 100,000 ounces per annum ... unless we do major capital works," Johnson said.
Telfer's continuing lower grades and higher costs have been compounded by heavy rains, which early this year cut the mine's access road and impaired production for 11 weeks.
"We didn't have an achievable plan before. We do now," he said.
Gold analyst Laurie Fitzgerald, of broker Hartley Poynton, said the market had expected Newcrest to slash its production forecast for Telfer but he was pleased to see Johnson take command.
"It's good to see Ian Johnson doing something about Telfer and grabbing the reins and getting cracking," he told Reuters.
Johnson was appointed chief executive in May, after the resignation of John Quinn whose last months in charge of the company were dogged by criticism over Telfer.
Quinn was also chief executive last year when Newcrest made a costly investment in fellow gold miner Normandy Mining Ltd in an aborted attempt to create a super gold company.
Johnson said he wanted to assure investors that Newcrest's future was brighter than its past.
"I think if we look to the future of this company, it's a pretty good outlook. If you look back, it's not so rosy."
-- Melbourne bureau 613-9286-1421
